content.title: Connection to SimplE+

content.comment:
Hi Bahare,

Thank you for your comment! [1] is a great work, adding taxonomic information to SimplE+ with non-negativity/ element-wise inequality constraints. We will cite this paper as related work during the revision period. 

Although [1] built upon SimplE, a method that was introduced more recently than TransH, we think our work differs from [1] in the following aspects:

1) For two relations “r1, r2”,  [1] requires constraints “if r1 -> r2”, but no constraint is imposed for the “only if” direction. Thus, [1] only guarantees monotonicity- that r1 is element-wise smaller than r2, and eventually, the mu((x, r1, y)) < mu((x, r2, y)) where mu is a score function for plausibility of fact triples. In other words, in [1] more general facts are just “more plausible.” 

On the other hand, TransINT guarantees that, if  “r1 -> r2” and “(x, r1, y)” is true, “(x, r2, y)” for all x, y, r1, r2. The entire motivation behind integrating external common sense/ taxonomic knowledge is that knowledge graphs cannot contain all true facts. Thus, our guarantee constraint, which automatically fills each missing but (potentially) true fact from existing ones, is more true to this motivation than the monotonicity constraint.  Experimental results support our claim. 

2) Here is an experimental comparison of TransINT and [1] (you can view the table if you click the link): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1auD5yPUsN92Uy0q5MIBO4H4UZBco0Ee9/view?usp=sharing.
TransINT outperformed [1] with large margins on both domains. Since [1] showed its effectiveness on NELL (Among the two datasets used in [1]), we chose to compare ourselves with [1] on NELL as well.

3) [1] is built on SimplE, which is a more recent method that is known to perform very well, when restricted to binary relations only. However, this method is not extendable to n-ary relations; SimplE creates n embeddings for each entity, which is not realistic when n is large. On the other hand, TransINT is extendable to any n-ary relation. This is because [2] showed that any n-ary relations can be equivalently considered as n binary relations, and empirically demonstrated that such an approach works under TransH. Similarly, TransINT can be extended to any n-ary relations with using the same model structure, by considering n-ary relations as n binary relations. Unlike SimplE or SimplE+, just 1 embedding vector is enough for each entity vector, regardless of n. 

4) TransINT’s real advantage lies in its semantic interpretability/ meta-learning that stems from its mapping of entity/relations as continuous sets of points. While TransH also does this, this point was never brought up before. Thus, our work is not an incremental addition to TransH, but a re-examination of TransH in a set-theoretic aspect that allows semantics learning at a higher level. 

We found the following error while reading [1]:

Table 1 is not logically consistent (error highlighted in red in this image: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Ow2hFgCKCcBWE4TB6MMCUlbWiL4hylEI/view?usp=sharing); it is impossible that Hit@10 is lower than Hit@3, because any entity that scores within “3” should automatically score within “10”. 

Again, we thank you for your comment!

[1] Fatemi, Bahare, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and David Poole. "Improved knowledge graph embedding using background taxonomic information." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 33. 2019.
[2] Wen, Jianfeng, et al. "On the representation and embedding of knowledge bases beyond binary relations." arXiv preprint arXiv:1604.08642 (2016).

content.review:
The authors propose TransINT, a novel graph embedding method that builds upon methods such as TransH (Knowledge graph embedding by translating on hyperplanes, Wang et al 2014), TransE (Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data, Bordes et al 2013), and appears to offer state of the art performance on the Freebase link prediction benchmark. 

The manuscript is OK overall in terms of writing (although it could use some copy editing for grammar) and relevant to this community. This reviewer is not familiar with knowledge graph embeddings, and found it difficult to follow the main ideas and contributions. The introduction could certainly be written in a clearer way, first stating the general problem and then building up from existing solutions to the proposed method. Many of the figure captures seem to contain typos (details below), making it particularly confusing to follow. The results appear impressive, but I will leave it to reviewers with more experience in the field to judge how it stacks up against recent work. 

Minor comments:
- In the first paragraph, there are two instances where closing brackets have been replaced by opening brackets. 
- Section 2, where transH is mentioned for the first time, it's missing a reference
- Incomplete sentence "Let ri be a binary relation x, y entities".
- Figure 2: h,t are not defined. is_family is mislabled as is_parent
-Figure 3: The line for is_parent_of is mislabeled as is_mother of.
-  Section 5, "We evaluate TransINT on Freebase 122 (respectively created by ...": What do you mean by "respectively" if there only Freebase 122 and no other dataset? Maybe forgot KALE here, it's mentioned a few sentences later for the first time and never defined.

content.review:
The paper presents a new embedding based system for Knowledge Graphs (KGs). The main characteristic of the proposed system is that it is able to preserve the subsumption hierarchy between relations in the embedding space.

The proposed system seems valid and technically sound to me. However I have two main concerns:
Presentation. The paper is full of typos (see [Details] below for some of them. The figures have several errors. TransE, TransH, TransR, KALE are cited without the references to the main papers. Moreover, it is rather confusing using the term relational space both for “relation vectors” and “relation hyperplane”. It seems the paper was written in a hurry and therefore it makes the paper hard to follow, it is a pity, because the proposed approach seems intriguing.
Experiments. The system was evaluated on a small dataset. It is not clear if the proposed system can scale.

For these reasons I think the paper is not ready for publication and that a revision is necessary.

[Details]
Page 1.
“R^dand”
“(.” twice at the end of a citation
Figure 2.
“viweing”
“His_family_of” is not defined anywhere
Figure 2b. 
It seems that all the relations are wrong
Page 4.
“(ex) A)”
“(ex) B)”
“space(Figure 3b)”
When Figure 4 is cited the symbols and the names used in the text does not match with the ones in the figure
“We evaluate TransINT on Freebase 122 (respectively created by Vendrov et al. and Guo et al.)”. These bibliographic citations do not make any sense. FB122 was released by Bordes et al.

[Minor]
There is too little space between the text and the captions of the figures.

content.review:
This paper proposes a way to enforce a partial ordering in the relation representations learned by a knowledge graph embedding model and outperforms KALE on FB122. However, it misses a larger set of related works in the knowledge graph learning literature and only compares on a subset of knowledge graph embedding tasks.

Major 
There is a number of related works missing in this paper:
One of the early papers incorporating logical constraints into knowledge graph embedding models is: Rocktäschel et al. Injecting Logical Background Knowledge into Embeddings for Relation Extraction. in: Proceedings of NAACL-HLT. 2015.
An approach that does this for relation embeddings by enforcing a partial ordering is: Demeester et al. Lifted Rule Injection for Relation Embeddings. in: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP). 2016
A recent method for incorporating logical constraints (such as partial ordering of relations) is: Minervini et al. Adversarial Sets for Regularised Neural Link Predictors. in: Proceedings of the 33rd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI). 2017 – a comparison to their numbers for FB122 should be added.
Most state-of-the-art knowledge graph embedding models are also evaluated on FB15K237 and WN18RR that is missing from this paper and makes comparison to prior work hard – see Lacroix, Timothée, Nicolas Usunier, and Guillaume Obozinski. "Canonical tensor decomposition for knowledge base completion." ICML 2018.
This is unrelated to the content of the paper, but in terms of style my suspicion is that the authors tinkered a lot with the LaTeX spacing in this submission. There are many places that look suspiciously crammed and squeezed together. This is not only violating the formatting instructions, but also makes the paper harder to read. Moreover, it seems also unnecessary as you could have gone up to 10 pages of main text. Moreover, citations are missing the year of the publication.

Minor
p1: The argument "cannot embed n-ary relations in KG's" is a) not true (see Minervini et al. 2017) above and b) your experiments are also only on binary relations in FB122.
p2: "such interpretable meta-learning opens up" – in what way is this meta-learning?

content.comment:
Thank you for your review. While it is true that the paper was rather brief on related work, we think it sufficiently explains where our work stands among the state-of-the-art. Among the works you mentioned in your comment([2],[3],[4],[5]), [2] is on relation extraction; also, KALE, which we compare to, is an extension of it. [3] models unary relations only and [4] models transitivity only (which is not strictly implication). Finally, while [5] is a recent method on embedding knowledge graphs, please note that our work is on embedding “knowledge graph with rules.” This is also the reason that restricts our work from being evaluated on FB15k23. Also, please note that, as in the comments, we have compared ourselves with [1] on NELL.  

In the future, we will add our evaluation on NELL and  clarify  to what kinds of datasets our methods are applicable. Furthermore, although we are clear enough on the comparisons with the state-of-the-arts that are in the same domain as our work, we plan to improve the thoroughness of  related work by clarifying the difference of our work to the ones you mentioned, and to improve organization and typography of the paper.

[1] Fatemi, Bahare, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and David Poole. "Improved knowledge graph embedding using background taxonomic information." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 33. 2019.

[2] Rocktäschel et al. Injecting Logical Background Knowledge into Embeddings for Relation Extraction. in: Proceedings of NAACL-HLT. 2015.

[3] Demeester et al. Lifted Rule Injection for Relation Embeddings. in: Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP). 2016

[4] Minervini et al. Adversarial Sets for Regularised Neural Link Predictors. in: Proceedings of the 33rd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI). 2017

[5] Lacroix, Timothée, Nicolas Usunier, and Guillaume Obozinski. "Canonical tensor decomposition for knowledge base completion." ICML 2018
